[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance defines how to derive structured, traceable requirements from authoritative sources — regulatory mandates, legacy systems, and enterprise standards — for domains where requirements cannot simply be elicited from stakeholders. It establishes a repeatable process for extracting, synthesizing, and reconciling requirement candidates from multiple authority sources, producing the inputs that BDD Discovery consumes.
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#business-value]

### Business Value

- **Reduces SME burden** — Subject matter experts review and validate structured material rather than authoring requirements from scratch
- **Ensures regulatory compliance** — Every requirement traces to its regulatory authority, enabling audit and demonstrating mandate coverage
- **Preserves institutional knowledge** — Legacy system behaviors are captured with source code provenance before modernization
- **Surfaces gaps and conflicts** — Cross-source analysis reveals where regulation mandates something the legacy system does not do, and where the legacy system does something without regulatory backing
- **Enables repeatable re-derivation** — When regulations change or source code is updated, the process re-enters at the appropriate step and produces delta metadata
page_texts.6:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#target-audience]

### Target Audience

| Audience | Uses This Guidance When... |
|----------|---------------------------|
| **Business Analysts** | Deriving requirements for a new bounded context in a regulated domain; standing up requirements for legacy modernization |
| **Product Owners** | Reviewing and deciding on synthesized requirement candidates; understanding why requirements exist (provenance) |
| **Architects** | Establishing BC boundaries before derivation; resolving cross-cutting conflicts during reconciliation |
| **AI Agents** | Executing derivation steps (regulatory extraction, source code analysis, synthesis); producing candidates in the standard format |
| **Compliance Officers** | Verifying that system requirements trace to regulatory mandates; auditing requirement coverage against CFR, state plans, and waivers |
page_texts.7:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#scope]

### Scope

This guidance covers the full requirements derivation lifecycle:

- **In scope:** Regulatory obligation extraction, source code behavior extraction, enterprise standard obligation extraction, cross-source synthesis, human reconciliation, snapshot versioning, and handoff to BDD Discovery
- **Out of scope:** Gherkin authoring (see BDD guidance), test design, implementation, deployment. This guidance produces requirements — it does not produce executable specifications.

page_texts.8:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#when-to-use-this-guidance]

## When to Use This Guidance

Use this process when requirements **cannot be invented by stakeholders alone** because the authoritative sources are external, complex, or encoded in existing systems.
page_texts.9:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#primary-use-cases]

### Primary Use Cases

| Situation | Why Standard Elicitation Fails | This Process Provides |
|-----------|-------------------------------|----------------------|
| **Regulated domains** (healthcare, finance, government) | Requirements come from CFR, state plans, waivers — not stakeholder preference | Systematic extraction of obligations from regulatory text with full citation chain |
| **Legacy modernization** | Requirements are implicit in existing code that nobody fully understands | Reverse engineering of behaviors with source code provenance |
| **Multiple conflicting authority sources** | Different sources (regulation vs. code vs. standards) disagree about what should happen | Synthesis that surfaces conflicts and a reconciliation gate that resolves them |
| **Multi-jurisdiction deployments** | The same capability must satisfy different regulatory interpretations per state/region | Two-tier model separating universal requirements from jurisdiction-specific parameters |
| **Audit-sensitive domains** | Regulators require evidence that system behavior traces to specific mandates | Provenance chain from requirement through derivation path to authority citation |
page_texts.10:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#when-not-to-use-this-guidance]

### When NOT to Use This Guidance

- **Greenfield product development** with no regulatory constraints — use standard stakeholder elicitation and BDD Discovery directly
- **Pure infrastructure** services with no domain regulation — requirements come from enterprise standards only (use the Applied Requirements path in isolation)
- **Small scope changes** to existing well-documented systems — if requirements already exist and are traceable, amend them directly

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#what-this-process-produces]

### What This Process Produces

- Requirement candidates with provenance (regulatory citation, source code location, or standard reference)
- A reconciled decisions register where a PO/architect has approved each candidate
- Finalized requirements in plain English with acceptance criteria — NOT Gherkin
page_texts.14:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#what-bdd-consumes]

### What BDD Consumes

- The finalized requirements from this process enter BDD at the **Discovery** phase (Example Mapping)
- The PO **validates** the requirements (they already have provenance and justification) rather than inventing them from scratch
- Example Mapping explores the edges and dimensions of each requirement
- Gherkin scenarios are authored downstream — this process does not produce them
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#why-requirements-and-gherkin-are-separate]

### Why Requirements and Gherkin Are Separate

In regulated domains:

1. **Stakeholders review requirements in plain language** — state agency reviewers sign off on policy compliance, not test cases
2. **Requirements must endure technology changes** — if requirements are Gherkin, every field rename triggers re-approval
3. **Combinatorial complexity** — regulated domains have dozens of interacting dimensions that no finite example set can cover; requirements state universal properties
4. **Governance stability** — requirements change when business needs change, not when implementation details change

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#derivation-paths]

## Derivation Paths

Three parallel derivation paths extract requirement candidates from different authority sources. Each path produces candidates in the same structural format, enabling synthesis to compare like-for-like.
page_texts.17:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#path-1-regulatory-derivation]

### Path 1: Regulatory Derivation

**Purpose:** Extract discrete obligations from regulatory text — what the law mandates the system must do.

**Authority sources:**

| Source Type | Examples |
|-------------|----------|
| Federal regulations | 42 CFR Parts 430-456 (Medicaid), 45 CFR 155-156 (Exchange), HIPAA |
| State plans | CMS-approved State Medicaid Plan attachments |
| State plan amendments (SPAs) | CMS-approved modifications to the state plan |
| Waivers | Section 1115, 1915(b), 1915(c) approved deviations |
| Sub-regulatory guidance | CMS Informational Bulletins, State Health Official letters |
| State administrative rules | State administrative code implementing Medicaid operationally |

**Process:**

1. **Scope identification** — Identify which regulatory sections govern this bounded context (constrained by BC boundary if established)
2. **Obligation extraction** — For each scoped section, extract every discrete obligation, permission, prohibition, and condition
3. **Interpretation** — Resolve ambiguities using guidance hierarchy; decompose compound obligations; apply waiver modifications
4. **Candidate production** — Each interpreted obligation becomes a requirement candidate with:
   - ID: `RC-{SCOPE}-NNN` (e.g., `RC-FED-001`, `RC-KS-001`)
   - Type: Business rule | Functional | Non-functional
   - Statement: Forward-facing, domain vocabulary, testable
   - Acceptance criteria: Observable behavior assertions
   - Regulatory chain: CFR section → state plan → waiver → guidance
   - Confidence: High | Medium | Low (with rationale)
5. **Gap analysis** — Identify CFR sections with no derived requirements (may indicate missed obligations or inapplicable sections)

**Key rules:**

- Extract at the level of individually testable obligations — one obligation per "shall" or "may"
- When a state plan narrows a federal option, capture both the federal baseline and the state election
- When a waiver modifies standard rules, note what changes and what remains
- Use regulatory language only — never use legacy system identifiers in obligation descriptions
- When regulations enumerate values, reference them as named classifications rather than inlining

**Output:** Immutable snapshot at `docs/requirements/_candidates/regulatory/{date}/`
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#path-2-legacysource-code-derivation]

### Path 2: Legacy/Source Code Derivation

**Purpose:** Extract system behaviors from existing implementations — what the system actually does today, expressed in domain language.

**Authority sources:**

| Source Type | Examples |
|-------------|----------|
| Source code | Stored procedures, ETL packages, service implementations |
| Existing tests | Test names and assertions (implicit acceptance criteria) |
| Configuration | Feature flags, config files, environment-specific settings |
| Database schema | Constraints, triggers, referential integrity rules |
| Operational data | Logs, metrics, incident history |

**Process:**

1. **Scope identification** — Define entry points, exclusions, and analysis depth
2. **Behavioral extraction** — For each module, extract discrete behaviors:
   - What the system does (in domain language, not code language)
   - Trigger conditions
   - Preconditions and postconditions
   - Error handling paths
   - Boundaries and thresholds
   - Code location (file, function, lines) for traceability
3. **Source system registration** — Record provenance: system name, state, source version, language, analysis date, pass identifier
4. **Requirement synthesis** — Transform behaviors into two-layer candidates:
   - **Top layer (forward-facing):** The requirement statement, acceptance criteria, and confidence — reads as if no legacy system exists
   - **Bottom layer (derivation context):** Source traces (module, file, function, lines, tables), legacy surface mappings, implementation notes — preserves full traceability
5. **Quality gate** — Every candidate's top layer must satisfy:
   - No legacy column/table names in requirement statements
   - No implementation algorithms (state outcomes only)
   - No vendor/system names as capability identifiers
   - Domain vocabulary from the BC's glossary
   - Acceptance criteria state observable behavior, not data format
6. **Gap identification** — Document untested behaviors, ambiguous intent, missing error handling

**Key rules:**

- Extract behavior, not implementation — say "stores the record" not "inserts into PostgreSQL"
- When code has conditional branches, each distinct path is a separate behavior entry
- Ignore pure infrastructure concerns unless they have domain-visible effects
- Flag behaviors where intent is unclear (could be a bug preserved as a feature)

**Output:** Immutable snapshot at `docs/requirements/_candidates/derived/{date}/`
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#path-3-applied-requirements-derivation]

### Path 3: Applied Requirements Derivation

**Purpose:** Extract obligations from enterprise standards, contractual SLAs, and organizational policies — requirements that exist beyond regulation and legacy code.

**Authority sources:**

| Source Type | Examples |
|-------------|----------|
| Enterprise standards | API standards, security standards, data modeling rules |
| Contractual terms | Response time SLAs, availability targets, data retention periods |
| Organizational policies | Data governance, incident response, operational requirements |
| Platform conventions | Observability requirements, deployment standards, API gateway rules |
| Professional judgment | Domain invariants that must be explicit in a service-boundary world |

**Process:**

1. **Source inventory** — Identify which enterprise standards, contract exhibits, and policies apply to this BC
2. **Obligation extraction** — For each source, extract testable obligations with:
   - Source citation (document, section, version)
   - Authority (who enforces: architecture review board, contract compliance, security team)
   - Obligation type (shall, should, conditional)
   - Measurability (how compliance is verified)
3. **Candidate synthesis** — Transform obligations into requirement candidates:
   - ID: `RC-APP-NNN`
   - Type: Business rule | Functional | Non-functional
   - Statement: Domain language, testable, implementation-agnostic
   - Acceptance criteria: Observable behavior assertions
   - Authority chain: Source document → section → enforcement mechanism
   - Confidence: High | Medium | Low
4. **Scope filtering** — Applied requirements represent business-visible obligations. Exclude:
   - Architecture-derived mechanics (idempotency, event ordering, replay) — these belong in tech specs
   - Team processes with no system-observable behavior
   - Design preferences without enforcement mechanism

**Litmus test for each candidate:**

1. "If removed, what measurable business-visible consequence occurs?" — If none observable to a non-technical stakeholder, it is not an applied requirement.
2. "Would a state program manager or contract compliance officer recognize this as an obligation?" — If only an architect would care, it belongs in tech specs.

**Output:** Immutable snapshot at `docs/requirements/_candidates/applied/{date}/`

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#cross-source-analysis]

### Cross-Source Analysis

When multiple derivation paths produce candidates for the same bounded context, synthesis performs cross-source analysis to identify relationships between them.

**Alignment categories:**

| Category | Description | Example |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| **Confirmed** | Same obligation from different sources (regulation + code agree) | CFR mandates X, legacy code does X — confirmed requirement |
| **Conflict** | Sources disagree about what should happen | Regulation says X, code does Y — needs reconciliation |
| **Regulatory gap** | Regulation mandates something the legacy system does not do | Novel obligation — system must be built to satisfy |
| **Code-only behavior** | Legacy system does something with no regulatory or enterprise mandate | May be undocumented business rule, may be tech debt |
| **Applied-only** | Enterprise standard imposes obligation the code does not yet satisfy | New obligation for modernized system |
| **Overlap** | Applied requirement restates a regulatory obligation | Regulatory candidate is authoritative; applied adds enforcement context |

**Cross-path comparison rules:**

- **Regulatory to Code:** Every regulatory candidate should have a corresponding code-derived candidate (the code implements the regulation). Missing alignment indicates either dead regulation (not implemented) or missed behavior extraction.
- **Applied to Code:** Every applied candidate should have a corresponding code-derived candidate. Missing alignment indicates a new obligation (standard published after the code) or missed extraction.
- **Code to Regulatory/Applied:** Code-derived candidates without regulatory or applied backing may be legitimate operational processes or indicate undocumented authority — flag for human classification.
page_texts.22:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#synthesis-register]

### Synthesis Register

Synthesis produces a single register (`_synthesis.md`) that consolidates all candidates from all paths with their cross-source alignment status. Each item in the register has:

| Field | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| ID | `SYN-NNN` — unique within the BC |
| Tier | Core (state-agnostic) or State-specific |
| Source refs | Which `RC-*` candidates from which paths contribute |
| Description | What the capability or obligation is |
| Cross-path alignment | Which paths agree and what each contributes |
| Classification | Business rule, functional, non-functional, integration context update, ADR candidate, deferred |
| Status | NEW, DECIDED, CHANGED, SUPERSEDED, BLOCKED |

**Status lifecycle:**

- `NEW` — first appearance, awaiting human decision
- `DECIDED` — human decided in Reconciliation (references decisions register)
- `CHANGED` — underlying analysis shifted since last decision, needs re-decision
- `SUPERSEDED` — no longer applicable (scope change, regulation repealed)
- `BLOCKED` — cannot proceed until external dependency is resolved

page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#decision-gate]

### Decision Gate

Reconciliation is the **human decision gate** between AI-assisted derivation and the deterministic pipeline that produces finalized requirements. No unresolved synthesis item may pass into the requirements step.

**Who decides:**

| Item Type | Decision Authority |
|-----------|-------------------|
| Standard functional requirements | Product Owner |
| Cross-cutting or boundary conflicts | Product Owner + Architect |
| Regulatory interpretation disputes | Product Owner + Compliance SME |
| Architecture-level tensions | Architect + Engineering Lead |
| Scope changes (adding/removing capabilities) | Product Owner + Architect |
page_texts.25:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#disposition-options]

### Disposition Options

For each NEW or CHANGED synthesis item, the decision-maker provides a disposition:

| Disposition | Meaning | Result |
|-------------|---------|--------|
| **INCLUDE** | This is a real requirement — proceed to finalization | Becomes a requirement with ID, type, and file location assigned |
| **EXCLUDE** | Not a requirement for this BC — out of scope | Documented with rationale; does not become a requirement |
| **DEFER** | Valid requirement but cannot resolve now | Documented with blocker, expected resolution, impact, and workaround |
| **AMEND** | An existing requirement partially covers this | Target requirement identified; acceptance criteria added |
| **MERGE** | Subset of another synthesis item | Consolidated into the target item |
| **SUPERSEDE** | Replaced by another decision | Linked to the replacing decision |
page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#conflict-resolution-hierarchy]

### Conflict Resolution Hierarchy

When derivation paths disagree:

| Conflict | Resolution Rule |
|----------|----------------|
| Regulation says X, code does Y | **Regulation wins.** Code divergence becomes tech debt or defect. |
| Waiver contradicts standard CFR | **Waiver wins** within its scope and duration. |
| State plan contradicts CMS guidance | **State plan wins** (CMS-approved). |
| Multiple regulations apply | Apply hierarchy: Waiver > State Plan > CFR > Sub-regulatory guidance. |
| Code does X, no mandate found | Human classifies: legitimate business rule (INCLUDE) or implementation artifact (EXCLUDE). |
| Enterprise standard contradicts regulation | **Regulation wins.** Standard is amended or exception documented. |

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#decisions-register-format]

### Decisions Register Format

Each reconciliation decision follows this structure:

```markdown
### DEC-NNN: {Title} ({DISPOSITION})

- **Synthesis item:** SYN-NNN
- **Disposition:** Include | Exclude | Defer | Amend | Merge | Supersede
- **Rationale:** {Why this decision was made — the justification}
- **Requirement type:** {Functional | Business Rule | Non-functional} (for INCLUDE only)
- **Requirement:** REQ-{BC}-{CAT}-NNN (for INCLUDE only)
- **Authority:** {Primary authority citation}
```

page_texts.32:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#immutability-rule]

### Immutability Rule

Derivation outputs are **immutable snapshots**. Once a derivation run produces candidates at `_candidates/{path}/{date}/`, that directory is never modified. Corrections, updates, or expansions produce a new snapshot.

**Date convention:** `{YYYY-MM-DD-NN}` where `NN` is a zero-padded sequence number for same-day runs (e.g., `2026-05-15-01`, `2026-05-15-02`).
page_texts.33:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#delta-protocol]

### Delta Protocol

When re-derivation occurs, the new snapshot includes delta metadata:

| Delta Type | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| **NEW** | Candidate that did not exist in prior snapshot |
| **CHANGED** | Candidate exists in prior snapshot but statement or acceptance criteria differ |
| **REMOVED** | Candidate existed in prior snapshot but is absent (obligation repealed, code deleted) |
| **UNCHANGED** | Candidate is identical to prior snapshot (carried forward for completeness) |

The synthesis step reads **all non-superseded snapshots** to build the current candidate set. When a new snapshot supersedes a prior one for the same derivation path, the synthesis register marks affected items as CHANGED (triggering re-decision in reconciliation).
page_texts.34:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#re-derivation-triggers]

### Re-Derivation Triggers

| Trigger | Re-enter At | Scope |
|---------|-------------|-------|
| New federal regulation (CFR update) | Regulatory derivation | Federal snapshot + affected state snapshots |
| State plan amendment approved | Regulatory derivation | Affected state snapshot only |
| Waiver granted, renewed, or expired | Regulatory derivation | Affected state snapshot |
| Source code updated (new release, defect fix) | Source code derivation | Affected module(s) |
| Enterprise standard published or updated | Applied requirements derivation | General snapshot |
| Contract amendment (new SLA terms) | Applied requirements derivation | General snapshot |
| New state onboarded | All paths | New state-specific snapshots |

**Lightweight re-entry:** Not every trigger requires the full process. Re-enter at the step that corresponds to what changed, then flow forward through synthesis and reconciliation.

page_texts.36:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#traceability-chain]

### Traceability Chain

Every requirement produced by this process must trace to its source authority through an unbroken chain:

```text
Finalized Requirement
  └─→ Decision (DEC-NNN in _decisions.md)
       └─→ Synthesis Item (SYN-NNN in _synthesis.md)
            └─→ Requirement Candidate (RC-*-NNN in snapshot)
                 └─→ Source Authority (citation, code location, or standard reference)
```

**Audit question this chain answers:** "Why does this requirement exist, and who says so?"
page_texts.37:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#per-path-provenance-formats]

### Per-Path Provenance Formats

Each derivation path has its own traceability format because the nature of the authority differs:

**Regulatory Derivation:**

```markdown
## Regulatory Authority

| Layer | Citation | Relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Federal | 42 CFR 435.403(a) | Creates the obligation |
| State Plan | Attachment 2.2-A, page 3 | Elects intent-to-reside standard |
| Waiver | §1115 KanCare 2.0, STC 21 | No modification |
| Guidance | CIB 2022-001 | Clarifies remote worker residency |

**Confidence:** High
```

**Source Code Derivation:**

```markdown
## Derivation Context

**Source system:**

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| System | {source system name} |
| State | {state abbreviation} |
| Source version | {build/branch/tag} |
| Language | {language(s)} |
| Analysis date | {YYYY-MM-DD} |
| Pass | {pass identifier} |

**Source traces:**

| Module | File | Function | Lines | Operation | Tables |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| {module} | {filename} | `{function_name}()` | {range} | {SELECT/INSERT/logic} | {table(s)} |

**Confidence:** {High | Medium | Low}
```

**Applied Requirements Derivation:**

```markdown

| Source | Section | Enforcement |
```

### Handoff to Discovery

After reconciliation produces finalized requirements, they enter the BDD lifecycle at the **Discovery** phase (Example Mapping). The handoff works as follows:

1. **Requirements with INCLUDE disposition** become inputs to Example Mapping sessions
2. The **acceptance criteria** in each requirement serve as pre-discovered Rules — the PO validates rather than invents from scratch
3. The PO, developer, and tester explore **dimensions** (axes of variation) within each requirement
4. Example Mapping produces concrete examples that become Gherkin scenarios downstream
page_texts.40:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#what-this-process-produces-vs-what-bdd-produces]

### What This Process Produces vs. What BDD Produces

| This Process Produces | BDD Produces |
|-----------------------|--------------|
| Universal property statements ("every beneficiary must be uniquely identifiable") | Concrete examples ("Given a beneficiary with SSN X and DOB Y...") |
| Plain-English acceptance criteria | Given/When/Then scenarios in Gherkin |
| Regulatory traceability (CFR → requirement) | Scenario tags linking to requirements (`@FR-NNN`) |
| Reconciled decisions with justification | Executable specifications with step definitions |
| Requirement candidates at the domain level | Test dimensions and boundary values |

**The boundary is clear:** This process answers "what must the system do and why?" BDD answers "what does that look like with specific examples and how do we prove it works?"
page_texts.41:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#pre-discovered-rules-in-example-mapping]

### Pre-Discovered Rules in Example Mapping

When requirements from this process enter Example Mapping, the Three Amigos session has a significant head start:

- **Rules** are largely pre-identified (the acceptance criteria from reconciled requirements)
- **Questions** focus on edge cases and dimension interactions rather than "what should the system do?"
- **Examples** explore boundaries of established rules rather than discovering rules from scratch
- The PO's role shifts from **inventing** requirements to **validating** that the derived requirements are correct and **exploring** their edges

This makes BDD Discovery significantly more efficient in regulated domains where the "what" is externally mandated.

## Roles and Responsibilities

| Role | Responsibility in This Process |
|------|-------------------------------|
| **Business Analyst** | Scopes derivation inputs; identifies which regulatory sections, code modules, and standards apply; reviews candidate quality; facilitates reconciliation sessions |
| **Product Owner** | Makes INCLUDE/EXCLUDE/DEFER decisions during reconciliation; validates that derived requirements match business intent; owns the decisions register |
| **Architect** | Establishes BC boundaries before derivation (constrains scope); resolves cross-cutting conflicts and boundary tensions; co-decides on architecture-level items |
| **AI Agent** | Executes derivation steps (regulatory extraction, code analysis, synthesis); produces candidates in standard format; performs cross-path alignment analysis |
| **SME (Subject Matter Expert)** | Validates regulatory interpretation; confirms whether code behavior is intentional or accidental; resolves ambiguities that AI cannot |
| **Compliance Officer** | Reviews regulatory derivation for completeness; verifies that mandate coverage is adequate; validates regulatory hierarchy application |

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md#anti-patterns]

## Anti-Patterns

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | Correct Approach |
|--------------|------------------|------------------|
| **Requirements as Gherkin** | Conflates requirements with test cases; triggers re-approval on field renames; stakeholders cannot review | Keep requirements in plain English; Gherkin lives downstream in the BDD lifecycle |
| **Single-source derivation** | Misses gaps (top-down only misses operational nuances; bottom-up only launders bugs into requirements) | Derive from multiple sources; reconcile the differences |
| **Skipping reconciliation** | AI-produced candidates go directly to implementation without human validation | Every candidate must pass through human decision gate before becoming a requirement |
| **Mutable snapshots** | Editing derivation outputs in place destroys the audit trail and makes delta detection impossible | Snapshots are immutable; corrections produce new snapshots |
| **Legacy identifiers in requirements** | Requirements become coupled to the old system; meaningless to greenfield implementers | Use domain vocabulary in the requirement; preserve legacy identifiers only in the derivation context |
| **PO invents rather than validates** | In regulated domains, requirements come from external authorities — PO validates derivation, not invents | Derive from authority sources; present PO with structured material to validate |
| **Conflating regulation with code behavior** | Assuming the legacy system correctly implements regulation when it may not | Derive from both independently; reconcile to surface divergence |
| **Orphaned provenance** | Requirements exist without traceability to their source authority | Every requirement must trace through the chain: requirement → decision → synthesis → candidate → authority |
| **Over-scoping derivation** | Analyzing all of 42 CFR when the BC only owns a narrow slice | Constrain derivation scope using BC boundary (integration context) before starting |
| **Skipping gap analysis** | Declaring derivation complete without checking for regulatory sections with no candidates | Run gap analysis after each path; surface uncovered sections explicitly |
